claims.text: Pulumi components let you turn a group of resources into a reusable building block that can be shared across projects and teams, and users work with the component's inputs and outputs without needing to understand every resource inside it.
The Pulumi components concept page exists at /docs/iac/concepts/components/.
The legacy AWSX VPC component manages the VPC, subnets, route tables, and gateways behind a few lines of code.
Pulumi's new component state migrations let a component author ship the upgrade path with the component itself.
A Pulumi component state migration translates the saved state of a component and its children before Pulumi works out which resources need to change.
Component authors can change a component's internal design and include the state migration in the same release.
The Pulumi state migrations API is experimental and may change.
A GitHub discussion for component state migrations feedback exists at https://github.com/pulumi/pulumi/discussions/24799.
The AWSX VPC state migration example exists at https://github.com/pulumi/examples/tree/master/aws-ts-awsx-vpc-state-migration and follows a network through v1, v2, and v3 versions of the code.
A Pulumi docs page on component state migrations exists at /docs/iac/guides/building-extending/components/state-migrations/ and covers the callback contract.
The v1 example uses the legacy `awsx.classic.ec2.Vpc` component.

In the v1 example, the legacy `awsx.classic.ec2.Vpc` component creates a VPC with one isolated subnet, a route table and its association, and an internet gateway, and a security group sits outside the component and refers to the VPC.
Without a migration connecting the old state to the new code, upgrading from the legacy AWSX VPC component could replace the VPC instead of keeping it.

Because the AWS security group refers to the VPC's ID, replacing the VPC would mean replacing the security group too (per the AWS CloudFormation EC2 SecurityGroup VpcId property documentation, which the post links).
The example does not create a database.
If a database itself has to be recreated, its replacement does not automatically contain the old data, and without a backup or data migration deleting the old database could mean losing that data.
The second version (v2) of the example upgrades to the modern `awsx.ec2.Vpc` component while keeping the existing network.
The third version (v3) of the example removes AWSX and declares the resources directly with `@pulumi/aws`.
Across all three versions of the example, the AWS resource IDs stay the same and the security group continues to use the same VPC.

In v1 of the example, Pulumi tracks the legacy component as `awsx:x:ec2:Vpc` with child `awsx:x:ec2:Subnet` and `awsx:x:ec2:InternetGateway` component records wrapping `aws:ec2/subnet:Subnet`, `aws:ec2/routeTable:RouteTable`, `aws:ec2/routeTableAssociation:RouteTableAssociation`, and `aws:ec2/internetGateway:InternetGateway` resources, with the subnet named `vpc-isolated-0`.

In v2 of the example, Pulumi tracks the modern component as `awsx:ec2:Vpc` with an `aws:ec2/vpc:Vpc` child, under which sit the subnet `vpc-isolated-1` (with route table and route table association nested beneath) and the internet gateway.

In v3 of the example, the resource tree is rooted at `aws:ec2/vpc:Vpc` with no awsx component records, holding subnet `vpc-isolated-1` (route table and association nested beneath) and the internet gateway.

Pulumi's state records both physical resources and the components that group them; each record has a Pulumi name called a URN, and managed resources also have an ID from the cloud provider such as an AWS VPC ID.
The legacy AWSX component wraps the subnet and internet gateway in separate components, while modern AWSX removes those wrappers and puts the managed resources under different parents.
In the example, the Pulumi name of the subnet changes from `vpc-isolated-0` to `vpc-isolated-1` between legacy and modern AWSX.
Pulumi aliases handle changes to a resource's name, type, or parent when its saved state remains compatible.
Aliases alone cannot remove component wrappers and transfer references to the resources that take their place; a state migration describes that whole change together.
The Pulumi resource aliases documentation exists at /docs/iac/concepts/resources/options/aliases/.
To migrate to modern AWSX, the new VPC component is registered with an alias for the legacy component type and a migration callback passed through the `stateMigrations` resource option.
`migrateClassicVpc` comes from the example's migration file at aws-ts-awsx-vpc-state-migration/v2/migration.ts.
With a state migration, the alias lets Pulumi find the old component, and the migration callback receives the old component's saved state followed by the state of its children.

A state migration callback returns two things: `newState`, the complete set of records that should replace the old component and its children, and `successors`, a map from each old URN that disappears to the URN that takes its place.
The full migration code for v2 is at aws-ts-awsx-vpc-state-migration/v2/migration.ts in pulumi/examples.

In the example's first migration callback, initial checks make it safe to run again: if the state already uses modern AWSX or plain AWS resources, it does nothing, and an unexpected component type raises an error instead of guessing.
The example's `rename` helper copies the saved record and changes its URN, type, and parent, preserving the AWS resource ID and other saved fields, and moves the subnet under the managed VPC.
The two subnet entries in `successors` tell the Pulumi engine that the old component wrapper and the managed subnet point to the same new subnet record.
Pulumi uses `successors` mappings to update dependencies and resource references elsewhere in the stack.
The VPC successor mapping keeps the security group's reference to the VPC connected to the migrated VPC record, which retains the same AWS VPC ID.
The third version of the example declares the VPC, subnet, route table, association, and internet gateway directly with `@pulumi/aws`.
The second migration changes who defines the resources in the program, and their configuration can be adjusted in a separate update.

The example's second migration (v3/migration.ts) removes the AWSX VPC component record and moves the managed VPC into its place; both the old component and its VPC child map to the new VPC record, the VPC keeps its AWS ID, and the other resources remain beneath it.
In v3 of the example, the VPC registration keeps aliases for both previous component types (legacy and modern AWSX VPC) and both migration callbacks.
Pulumi runs multiple state migration callbacks in order, passing each callback's result to the next callback.
A stack still using legacy AWSX can upgrade directly to the plain AWS version, and a stack already using modern AWSX skips the first migration.
Once both migrations have run, both callbacks return no result on later updates.
Keeping earlier migrations with the component means its users can skip versions without having to edit stack state by hand.
After a state migration changes saved state, Pulumi compares the new program with that state and calls the provider for any remaining changes.
In this example, the upgrades can still show in-place updates for provider defaults and tags even though resource IDs are kept.
To try the example, start with the `v1` directory and follow its README, using the same stack, backend, project name, AWS region, and availability zone for each version.
Before each upgrade in the example, `pulumi preview` should show no creates, deletes, or replacements for the existing VPC, subnet, route table, association, internet gateway, and security group.
`pulumi preview` evaluates the state migration without saving it, and `pulumi up` saves the migrated state.

When a component registers a state migration inside its implementation, users do not need to write the migration, attach the callback, or edit their stack state; when they upgrade the component and run Pulumi, it runs the migration as part of the normal preview and update.
For an internal component change that keeps the same component inputs and outputs, users can keep their existing component calls without knowing which resources moved or how saved state changed.
The VPC example in pulumi/examples contains all three programs (v1, v2, v3) and the migration code shown in the post.
Pulumi state migration callbacks (the `stateMigrations` resource option) run during both previews and updates when prior state exists for the resource.
Pulumi state migration callbacks (the `stateMigrations` resource option) must be idempotent.
A Pulumi state migration callback must return no result when the resource state no longer needs migration.
Pulumi state migration callbacks rewrite resource state without performing provider operations.
A Pulumi component state migration is a pure function that transforms the saved state of a component and its children into the state expected by a new component version.
A Pulumi component state migration callback returns the updated state records and successor mappings.
In a Pulumi component state migration result, each successor mapping connects an old URN that is omitted from the result to the URN of the returned resource that takes its place.
If no migration is needed, a Pulumi component state migration callback returns no result.
The Pulumi option reference for stateMigrations at /docs/iac/concepts/resources/options/statemigrations/#callback-api explains the callback API.
The state entries passed to a Pulumi component state migration callback use the checkpoint resource format documented in the Pulumi developer docs deployment schema (pulumi-resource-state).
Pulumi checkpoint resource state entries include fields such as `urn`, `type`, `id`, `parent`, `provider`, `inputs`, and `outputs`.
A Pulumi component state migration callback that returns no result can remain attached when using update plans or targeted updates.
For Pulumi component state migrations, the restrictions on state-changing results (with update plans or targeted updates) do not require removing an already-applied migration.
